title: Go to the Land I Will Show You
lead: Sometimes hope begins with a step into the unknown.
questions: What step of faith is God calling you to that you keep putting off, waiting until you can see the whole road?
If you measured the past year of your life in altars instead of miles, how much of it would be left?
What have I received from God that has turned into a burden in me because it stopped flowing on to others?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: The last time God spoke, it was at the Tower of Babel, and it was a verdict. Then silence fell. The first word to break it is “Leave.” Adam was given a chance, and it ended in the flood. Noah was given a fresh start, and it ended at the Tower of Babel. The call of Abram opens a third stage, and this time it begins with one man. In chapters 1–11 a curse is pronounced five times. In the two verses of the call, blessing is spoken of five times.

God gives just one command: go. Everything else is promise: I will make you, I will bless you, I will make your name great. The builders of Babel wanted to win a name with their own hands: “that we may make a name for ourselves.” Abram receives a promise: “I will make your name great.” Here are two ways to succeed: fame that is seized and fame that is given.

The command tightens like a noose: leave your country, your kindred, your father’s household. And at the end there is no address, only a promise: “to the land I will show you.” Abram was seventy-five years old, and he went out “without knowing where he was going.” In the Bible, hope seldom begins with certainty. It usually begins with a step of faith. We would like to reverse the order: first see the whole road, and only then believe. Abram saw only the first stretch. And there is a play on words in this story: God promised a land He would “show” him, literally, let him see; and when Abram arrived, “the LORD appeared to Abram,” literally, let Himself be seen. He set out to see a land, and he saw God.

Right after that came a famine, and Abram fled to Egypt, where out of fear he passed off his wife as his sister. It is not God who rebukes him but Pharaoh, with questions that sound straight out of Eden: “What have you done to me? Why didn’t you tell me…?” The Bible doesn’t whitewash its heroes. But the most important thing is what this scene does not contain: the call is not withdrawn. Abram’s mistakes did not cancel the promise. The story shows that God remained faithful in spite of his stumble.

And then there is the direction: “All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” From its very first sentence, being chosen points outward. It isn’t a rank; it’s a task. A blessing that flows nowhere becomes a burden.

For the first two days we talked about disasters: the garden where everything broke and the water that carried off the whole world. Today we begin a new chapter: stories of people who were a long way from seeing a promise fulfilled. A very long way. The man we will be reading about over the next few days heard the promise that a son would be born to him and waited twenty-five years for that son. But before the waiting began, something even harder had to happen. He had to get moving.

sections.heading: The First Word After the Silence
paragraphs: The last time God spoke, He pronounced a verdict at the Tower of Babel. Then the story falls silent. Genealogies roll on, generations pass, and God says nothing. And suddenly the silence is broken: “Then the LORD said to Abram, ‘Leave…’” God’s first word after Babel is not a commentary on the disaster. It is an invitation to the road.

What exactly is being promised? Land, descendants, and God’s presence: precisely the three things humanity received at creation and lost outside the garden gate. Adam was driven out of paradise, death entered the world, and instead of walking with God, he hid from Him in the bushes. The call of Abram isn’t a new project. It is the beginning of recovering everything that was lost in Eden, and that is why the Bible places it right after eleven chapters of loss.

Look at where in the big story this sentence falls. Adam was given a chance, and it ended in the flood. Noah was given a fresh start, and it ended in scattering at the tower. Two starts for humanity, two falls. The call of Abram is the third attempt, but this time God changes His method: He doesn’t start with all of humanity, but with one man. The Creator’s words also tell us a lot. In chapters one through eleven a curse is pronounced five times. In the two verses of Abram’s call, blessing is spoken of five times. God rebalances the world’s accounts through one man.

sections.heading: Five Times “I,” One Command
paragraphs: Let’s read this speech carefully: “Leave your country, your kindred, and your father’s household, and go to the land I will show you. I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing.” In this whole speech there is exactly one command: go. Everything else is promise coming from God’s own mouth: I will make, I will bless, I will make great. The next verse adds two more declarations: I will bless and I will curse. Five verbs with God as “I,” one command for the man. Those are the proportions of this call, and they reflect the way the Most High approaches humanity throughout the history of salvation.

To feel the weight of this scene, we need to remember what the religion Abram grew up in was like. The gods of Mesopotamia didn’t reveal their intentions. No one knew for sure what would please them and what would make them angry, so they were worshiped the way one handles an unpredictable ruler: with flattery, bribery, and appeasement. Religion was the art of managing whims. And into that world comes a God who does something unheard of: He introduces Himself, says what He wants, and binds Himself with a promise; in other words, He gives a human being something to hold Him to later. This God doesn’t want to be serviced. He wants to be known.

There is also a deliberate jab at Babel in these words. The builders of the tower said, “Let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens, that we may make a name for ourselves.” They wanted to build a reputation with their own hands. Abram’s reputation is given to him as a gift: “I will make your name great.” These are two roads to success that have competed in every human life ever since: fame that is seized and fame that is given. Faith on one side, the tower on the other.

sections.heading: A Step into the Unknown
paragraphs: The command tightens like a noose: leave your country, then your kindred, then your father’s household. Three steps, and each one hurts more. At the end of the list stands not an address, but a promise: “to the land I will show you.” Future tense. At the moment he leaves, Abram doesn’t know where he is going, and the New Testament says so plainly: he went, “without knowing where he was going.”

In the process, the command strips away, one by one, all the layers of identity by which that world defined a person: land, clan, father’s house. In a world where you were where you came from, Abram was to become a man defined solely by where he had been sent. From that moment on, we see him living out his calling: with nothing behind him, on the road, dependent on the word.

He was seventy-five years old. That is not an age for starting over, and that is exactly why this story stands at the beginning of a section about promises that are a long way off. In the Bible, hope seldom begins with certainty. It usually begins with a step of faith. We would like to reverse the order: first see the whole road, then promise to set out. Abram saw only the first stretch, up to the edge of the known world. The rest was God’s word.

sections.heading: He Went to See a Land and Saw God
paragraphs: There is a hidden play on words in this promise that English translations barely hint at. God says, the land I will show you, literally, the land I will let you see. And when Abram reaches Shechem, the text says, “Then the LORD appeared to Abram,” literally, let Himself be seen. It is the same Hebrew verb. Abram was supposed to see a land, and he saw God. The goal of the journey turned out to be not a place, but the One who was waiting for him there.

From then on, the promise returns, more specific each time. First: the land I will show you. Then, at Shechem: I will give this land to your offspring. Then: all the land that you see. Finally: as an everlasting possession. God isn’t repeating Himself for lack of new material. He gives out light in step with the road: each stretch you travel uncovers another piece of the map. Whoever wants to know the whole plan before the first step will never know it, because it is revealed along the way.

For now Abram receives nothing. He buys no field, enters none of the cities, lives in a tent under the oaks. The Bible doesn’t record all his stops. It records the ones where he built an altar: Shechem, then near Bethel, then Mamre. Abram’s life is measured in altars, not miles. That is a good measure for our journeys too: not how far we have come, but where along the way we stopped with God.

sections.heading: A Faith That Could Not Survive Hunger
paragraphs: And then, right after the altar, comes a sentence that hurts: “Now there was a famine in the land. So Abram went down to Egypt.” The man who had just heard God’s voice leaves the land of promise because there is nothing to eat. And in Egypt, out of fear, he passes off his wife as his sister.

Geography offers a hint here. Canaan drinks water from the sky: if the rain doesn’t come, famine follows. Egypt has the Nile: water always flows there, whatever the sky does. Canaan is a land where you have to trust. Egypt is a land where everything is visible. Abram’s faith survived a foreign land and foreign people. It did not survive an empty granary.

The bitterest part is the end of the scene. It isn’t God who rebukes Abram. Pharaoh does, and with questions that echo those in the garden of Eden: “What have you done to me? Why didn’t you tell me…?” A pagan speaks to the chosen one in the words God once spoke to Adam. And the chosen one doesn’t answer a word. The Bible doesn’t whitewash its heroes, and that is one of the things that makes it most believable.

There is one more lesson in this account, uncomfortable and necessary. Abram went down to Egypt right after he had seen God and built Him two altars. An experience of God, even the most genuine, does not make us immune to fear. Great spiritual experiences and great acts of cowardice can fit into the same week. Whoever doesn’t know this will judge others for every collapse after a spiritual high. Whoever knows it is more careful, with others and with themselves. And the narrator adds a quiet punch line: Abram came out of Egypt richer by flocks and silver, and still childless. You can come back with loaded camels and empty hands at the same time.

The most important thing in this scene is what isn’t there. There is no withdrawal of the call. God doesn’t say: well then, I’ll find someone else. Abram’s wavering did not cancel the promise. It only delayed its fulfillment. This is a sentence worth taking away from today’s reading and keeping in reserve, because it will be needed many more times, both in this series and in life: our stumbles can delay the fulfillment of God’s promises. They cannot revoke them.

sections.heading: You Will Be a Blessing
paragraphs: One more sentence from the call remains, the widest one: “All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” From the very first moment, Abram’s election points outward. He is not chosen out of the nations in order to wall himself off from them, but in order to bring them something. “You will be a blessing” isn’t a compliment; it’s a job description.

The fate of this promise later in the story is full of irony. The great nation announced on the day of the call was ultimately born in Egypt: seventy people went there during a famine, and it was there, with no land, no freedom, and no prospect of either, that this handful grew into a people. God’s promises don’t wait for favorable conditions. They can come true in places that look like their very contradiction.

The difference between rank and task seems small, but it decides everything. Election understood as rank raises the question: who is in and who is out? Election understood as a task forces us to ask: to whom are we supposed to carry something? For long centuries Israel could confuse the one with the other and paid a high price for it. We are not free of that mistake. The test isn’t what we declare, but whether anything flows through us to people who don’t belong to us. A blessing that doesn’t flow onward stops being a blessing. It becomes a burden.

Finally, there is a promise in this sentence for us, the readers, too. If all the families of the earth were to be blessed in Abram, then on the day of his call God was also thinking of people who would read this story four thousand years later, wherever in the world they happen to live. None of us is a chance guest in this story.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: Of the three things promised to Abram, two kept him waiting for decades: descendants and land. The third, God’s presence, he experienced from the very first day. And it didn’t disappear even when Abram lost his nerve in Egypt. That is the structure of a life lived with a promise: you often have to wait for its fulfillment, but the One who gave it walks beside you from the first step. If today you are facing a decision and can see only the first stretch of the road, this story says: that is enough. Abram didn’t see any more than that either.
